newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - BASF is new target in sick pay protests.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BASF is new target in sick pay protests.

text.p: Fierce union protests over German companies' plans to cut sick payments spread to the chemical sector on Wednesday as 13,000 workers walked off the job at chemical giant BASF AG.

BASF AG said on Tuesday it would cut sick pay to 80 percent of the normal wage from November 1 from 100 percent currently, controversially implementing a new law just one day after several car firms reversed a decision to take the same action.

The company, which seemingly risks isolation on the issue, found welcome backing from the BDA umbrella organisation of Germany employers associations, which stated that sick pay cuts should be imposed where possible.

Employers believe that wage contracts in the chemical industry have been drafted in such a way that the cuts can be enforced now, avoiding the legal row that followed attempts by engineering groups to do the same.

But BASF worker representatives said they were as determined to resist the cuts as their counterparts in the metal and engineering sector, which last week saw protests across the country involving over 120,000 workers.
"This is the start of a hot autumn (of protest)," Volker Obenauer, head of the BASF works council told a rally at BASF's headquarters in the industrial town of Ludwigshafen.
He threatened an overtime ban, and warned the workers would stage further protests over the next few days.

BASF's decision to cut sick pay -- implementing a new federal law passed last month -- came hot on the heels of a decision by companies led by Daimler-Benz AG to drop similar plans in response to widespread worker protest.
Those companies have now agreed not to put the cuts into effect for the time being, pending further agreements with unions.

Although BASF said in its statement that its final decision on the cuts would also depend on the outcome of a meeting with unions on October 25, the workers saw the pre-announcement as an aggressive move which pre-empted their talks.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, representatives of BASF's works council and the local branch of chemical union IG Chemie said they were "angry and disappointed" at BASF's decision and described it as a "slap in the face" for loyal workers.

The unions have argued forcefully that any change in benefits must be agreed in negotiation. They see a one-sided management decision to adopt the new law as an attack on free collective bargaining as it does away with hard-won benefits.
But employer representatives such as BDA are equally determined that labour costs are too high in Germany and must be reduced.

Speaking to journalists in Bonn, BDA chief executive Reinhard Goehner said the ruling should be carried out but said there was possible flexibility depending on how the wage basis for calculating sick pay is determined.

Taking up this theme, Gerhard Zambelli, regional head of the engineering union IG Metall in Baden-Wuerttemberg, said that overtime work pay could cease to be included in calculations for sick pay benefits.
BASF itself has suggested that the planned sick pay cut could be achieved by employees foregoing one regular day of holiday for every five sick days.

Talks over sick pay in the engineering sector are due to resume on Thursday between IG Metall and the Gesamtmetall industrial employers group. IG Metall has also announced its call for a 1997 pay increase of between 4.5 and five percent.
